questions.q: The magnitude of the force experienced by a charge travelling through a magnetic field is given by F = qvB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the velocity and the field lines. What does this equation tell you about the force?
options: The force is a maximum when the velocity of the charge is parallel to the field lines
The force is a maximum when the velocity of the charge is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines, and reduces to zero when the velocity is parallel to the field lines
The force is constant for all angles between the velocity and the field lines
The force is a maximum when the velocity is parallel and zero when the velocity is perpendicular to the field lines
questions.explanation: In F = qvB sin θ, θ is the angle between the velocity and the field lines. When the velocity is perpendicular to the field, θ = 90°, sin θ = 1 and the force is its maximum value qvB; when the velocity is parallel, θ = 0, sin θ = 0 and the force reduces to zero.

questions.q: Using F = qvB sin θ, in which situation does a charge in a magnetic field experience no force?
options: When the charge moves perpendicular to the magnetic field lines
A motionless charge in a magnetic field, or a charge that moves along the field parallel to the field lines, experiences no force
When the charge has a large velocity across the field
When the charge is a positive alpha particle rather than a negative electron
questions.explanation: If v = 0 then F = qvB sin θ = 0, so a motionless charge in a magnetic field experiences no force. If the velocity is parallel to the field lines then θ = 0, sin θ = 0, so a charge that moves along the field also experiences no force.

questions.q: When alpha and beta radiation particles are released into the same magnetic field, describe how each particle is deflected and why the beta particle follows the tighter circular arc.
keyPoints: The alpha particle is a relatively heavy, positively charged helium ion; applying the right-hand push rule, it is pushed upwards along a circular arc.
The beta particle is a comparatively low mass, negatively charged electron, so it is forced downwards along a much tighter circular arc.
The smaller mass of the electron causes the smaller radius of its arc; the force acts as a centripetal force creating circular motion.
questions.explanation: The sign of the charge sets the direction of deflection (alpha up, beta down) and the mass sets the size of the circle — the low-mass electron has the smaller radius. If you recalled both the direction and the mass-radius link, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: To derive the radius of the circular motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field, the only significant force is the magnetic force F = qvB, acting as a centripetal force. Equating it to mv²/r gives which expression for the radius?
options: r = Bq / (mv)
r = mv / (Bq)
r = mvB / q
r = qvB / m
questions.explanation: The magnetic force qvB provides the centripetal force, so qvB = mv²/r. Cancelling one factor of v gives qB = mv/r, and rearranging for the radius gives r = mv/(Bq). A greater mass or velocity increases the radius, while a greater charge or field strength decreases it.

questions.q: An electron travelling at 5.9 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a magnetic field of 6.0 mT. What is the radius of its circular path?
questions.explanation: Straight application of r = mv/Bq, using the magnitude of the electron's charge. Watch the millitesla conversion: 6.0 mT = 6.0 × 10⁻³ T, not 6. The tiny radius (5.6 mm) reflects how easily the feather-light electron is turned.

questions.q: A stream of electrons with a velocity of 1.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of strength 2.6 × 10⁻³ T at right angles. Calculate the magnitude of the force that the field exerts on each electron.
questions.explanation: Because the electron enters at right angles, θ = 90° and the force is simply qvB. A tiny force, but acting on a far tinier mass, so it bends the path hard. This is part (a) of the textbook's 4.3 Exercise question.

questions.q: From the expression r = mv/Bq for the radius of the circular path, how does the radius of the circular motion depend on the particle's mass, velocity, charge and the magnetic field strength?
options: A greater mass or velocity will decrease the radius, while a greater charge or field strength will increase it
A greater mass or velocity will increase the radius, while a greater charge or magnetic field strength will decrease the radius of the circular path
Only the charge affects the radius; mass, velocity and field strength have no effect
A greater velocity decreases the radius because faster particles turn more sharply
questions.explanation: Reading r = mv/Bq directly: mass and velocity are on the top, so a greater mass or velocity increases the radius; charge and field strength are on the bottom, so a greater charge or magnetic field strength decreases the radius. The trap is thinking more force means a bigger circle — a stronger field gives a tighter circle.

questions.q: Comparing the effect of electric and magnetic fields on a moving charge, which statement correctly distinguishes the force and the trajectory in each case?
options: Both an electric field and a magnetic field exert a force directed along the field, and both produce a parabolic trajectory

An electric field exerts a force directed along the field and produces a parabolic trajectory, while a magnetic field exerts a force perpendicular to the field and the velocity and produces a circular trajectory
An electric field produces a circular trajectory, while a magnetic field produces a parabolic trajectory
A magnetic field exerts a force on a stationary charge directed along the velocity, producing a straight-line trajectory
questions.explanation: An electric field exerts a force on a charge directed along the field and produces a parabolic trajectory. A magnetic field exerts a force only on a charge already moving across the field, directed perpendicular to both the field and the velocity, and produces a circular trajectory.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why a magnetic force can change the direction of a charged particle's motion but cannot change its speed.
keyPoints: The magnetic force is always directed perpendicular to the velocity of the charge at every instant.
Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force; a force perpendicular to the motion does no work, so the kinetic energy and therefore the speed stay constant.
The force does continually change the direction of the velocity — it is a centripetal force — so the direction changes even though the speed does not.
questions.explanation: The band-six phrasing names every step: perpendicular force, does no work, constant speed and kinetic energy, but direction continually changes. If you only said 'the magnetic force accelerates it', grade Again or Hard — that misses that the speed is untouched.

questions.q: The period of a charged particle's circular motion in a uniform magnetic field works out to T = 2πm/qB. What does this result tell you, and why is it the key to the cyclotron?
options: The period grows with speed, so faster particles take longer to go round
The speed v cancels, so the period is independent of speed — a faster particle just draws a proportionally larger circle in the same time, letting the cyclotron use one fixed timing
The radius is independent of speed, so all particles trace the same-sized circle
The period depends only on the speed, not on the mass, charge or field
questions.explanation: Substituting r = mv/qB into T = 2πr/v cancels the speed entirely, leaving T = 2πm/qB — the period depends only on mass, charge and field. A faster particle follows a larger circle but covers it faster, so the time per loop is unchanged; the cyclotron exploits this by kicking the particle at a fixed frequency. Note it is the period, not the radius, that is independent of speed.
